### Audit middleware that never blocks the real write — best-effort logging done right

URL: https://portfolio-seven-opal-35.vercel.app/notes/audit-middleware-never-blocks-real-write
Date: 2026-05-14. 6 min read.

Pilates Studio's audit middleware records every admin write — actor, resource, IP, user-agent, before/after diff — to `audit_log` table. Audit insert is best-effort: failures logged locally, real operation still commits. Losing a booking because audit insert was slow is not acceptable user-facing behavior.

Wrong design: wrap every write in a transaction, audit insert inside, audit failure rolls back real write. Right design: route handler completes normally + commits, middleware runs after, computes audit payload, fires INSERT, catches errors, moves on. 99%+ complete audit log; recoverable gaps; user never blocked.

When you need stronger guarantees (healthcare, finance, regulatory audit): use background-queued audit writes — durable queue, retry until audit row exists. Pilates Studio doesn't have that requirement; best-effort sidecar is right tradeoff. Pattern generalizes to any sidecar concern (analytics events, notification dispatch, webhook outbound calls) that shouldn't fail the main operation. Be explicit which concerns are critical-path.

### Booking-flow status transitions — auto-promoting from the waitlist on cancellation

URL: https://portfolio-seven-opal-35.vercel.app/notes/booking-flow-status-transitions-waitlist
Date: 2026-05-14. 6 min read.

Pilates Studio booking states: pending → confirmed → attended | cancelled → refunded. Waitlist states: waiting → promoted | expired. Postgres enums via Prisma; every transition logged for audit reconstruction.

Auto-promotion: when confirmed → cancelled, same transaction runs follow-up — find oldest `waiting` entry for same class, atomically transition to `promoted`, create `confirmed` booking row, fire confirmation email + SMS within seconds. Atomicity matters: two simultaneous cancellations would otherwise both try to promote the same waitlist entry. Postgres serializes; exactly one promotion per cancellation.

Cron sweep (every 5 min) belt-and-suspenders for missed real-time promotions. Promoted member gets two-hour cancellation window; if they cancel, seat goes back to waitlist for next-up member (same logic, different trigger). Operator never manually reshuffles attendance. "Runs itself" is the whole point of SaaS for one-location boutique studio. Pattern generalizes to any queue with priority order + capacity constraints — restaurant reservations, conference workshops, therapy sessions.

### Discipline as the product — architectural rules that survive every refactor

URL: https://portfolio-seven-opal-35.vercel.app/notes/discipline-as-the-product
Date: 2026-05-14. 7 min read.

CleanSlate's product is the architectural discipline. Rules enforced structurally — TypeScript types + ESLint imports + RLS policies, not conventions:

(1) Route files dispatch — they don't do. Every Next.js route is two lines (parse input, call service, return response). Services do the work. Boundary enforced because there's nowhere else to put logic.

(2) Services own all data ops. No Supabase calls outside services folder. ESLint no-restricted-imports blocks components from importing the Supabase client at compile time. Architectural enforcement beats discipline-enforcement.

(3) Money is always cents. €20 plan = 2000. Stored, transmitted, operated on as integer cents. TypeScript branded type `Cents = number & { __brand: 'Cents' }` makes wrong-type compile errors. Display formatting at UI boundary.

(4) Phones are E.164. `+49301234567` always. Validation rejects non-E.164 at boundary. Display formatting at UI.

(5) RLS scopes every query. `auth.uid()` filter on every Supabase policy. `from('jobs').select()` doesn't need `.eq('user_id', userId)` — policy adds it.

(6) `(marketing)` vs `(app)` route groups in Next 16. Structurally impossible to render marketing pages requiring auth or auth pages on marketing domain.

Customer pays for software working reliably for 3 years, not for architectural discipline. The discipline makes that promise affordable to keep.

### Four Vercel cron endpoints — the minimum for a SaaS that runs itself

URL: https://portfolio-seven-opal-35.vercel.app/notes/four-vercel-crons-saas-runs-itself
Date: 2026-05-14. 6 min read.

CleanSlate's operator never logs in for routine admin. Four crons handle everything: (1) trial-reminders daily — finds users in 3-day window before trial end + emails; (2) overdue-invoices daily — nudges `past_due` subscriptions + auto-cancels after 3 nudges (then RLS gate prevents new writes); (3) recurring-jobs daily — generates next week's bookings from active recurring schedules; (4) pre-job-sms hourly — sends reminders for jobs within 24h, marks confirmed.

Idempotency is the discipline. Every cron must be runnable twice in a row without wrong results. Vercel retries on failure; non-idempotent handlers produce duplicates. Strategies: upsert by stable keys (client_id + scheduled_date), per-record last-action timestamps, per-action confirmed flags. Cron auth via shared secret in Authorization header (Vercel includes automatically); unauthorized requests get 401.

Why cron not queue: these are periodic sweeps of database state, not event-triggered jobs. State is the trigger. Queues (BullMQ, Trigger.dev) are right when events drive work; crons are right for "sweep state space periodically and act on what matches." Operator-hours-per-customer is the SaaS scaling cap. Four crons removes that cap for routine ops.

### MMKV vs AsyncStorage on the cold-start hot path — when synchronous storage wins

URL: https://portfolio-seven-opal-35.vercel.app/notes/mmkv-vs-asyncstorage-cold-start-hot-path
Date: 2026-05-14. 6 min read.

AsyncStorage's `getItem(key): Promise<string | null>` crosses the JavaScript-to-native bridge on every read. Cold-start sequence with auth + draft + recent state needs 5-6 reads minimum — 20-50ms of bridge waits before UI can do anything useful. Loading screen between launch and first useful render gives users impression of slowness.

MMKV (Tencent's mobile key-value store + Marc Rousavy's `react-native-mmkv` binding) is synchronous + encrypted + memory-mapped. `mmkv.getString('auth')` returns immediately, no promise. ~30x faster than AsyncStorage. Dabei uses MMKV for auth (session token, user ID, name), draft hangouts (partially-composed state), last-known map region (lat/lng + zoom), recently-viewed hangouts ring buffer.

What doesn't go in MMKV: bulk data (lists, full profiles, message history — belongs in Supabase + React Query cache), hardware-backed secrets (refresh tokens, biometric keys — belongs in expo-secure-store on iOS keychain). Migration: lazy — check MMKV first, fallback to AsyncStorage if missing, copy + delete. Self-cleaning over a few app launches. Don't aggressive-migrate.

Expo support: works in bare workflow + EAS dev client; doesn't work in Expo Go (requires native linking). Dabei uses EAS dev client specifically because MMKV is non-negotiable for cold-start UX.

### Vibe Checks as a first-class entity — when a social mechanic is the product

URL: https://portfolio-seven-opal-35.vercel.app/notes/vibe-checks-first-class-entity
Date: 2026-05-14. 7 min read.

Dabei's vibe check is a one-tap rating any attendee can submit during or up to 48 hours after a hangout. Trinary (good/neutral/off), optional comment. Stored as rows in `vibe_checks` table with unique constraint on (submitter_id, target_id, hangout_id).

`submit_vibe_check` Postgres RPC enforces atomically: submitter is verified attendee (RSVP + check-in), hangout has ended or is ongoing, within 48-hour window, no existing rating from this submitter for this target/hangout, target was at the hangout. All checks in one transaction; race conditions impossible because Postgres serializes.

`profiles.is_trusted` flips to true automatically when user accumulates 15+ positive vibe checks from 10+ unique people. Unique-people requirement matters — without it, one friend rating 15 times = trusted. With it, real popularity required. Implemented as Postgres trigger on `vibe_checks` table that recomputes target stats after every insert.

Trinary not stars: star ratings inflate (everyone is 4.7). Trinary preserves distinction + lower submission friction + meaningfully higher participation rate. Aggregate displayed on profile, not individual ratings — naming who downvoted is unhelpful and harmful. Pattern generalizes to attendance-verified reputation in any app where shared experiences are the trust signal.

### Splitting the data layer into reads, writes, and actions — the three-services pattern

URL: https://portfolio-seven-opal-35.vercel.app/notes/three-services-data-layer-hangout-crud-queries-actions
Date: 2026-05-14. 7 min read.

Dabei's hangout data layer is three small services instead of one 1500-line god-service: `hangout-crud` (writes — create, update, delete with Zod validation), `hangout-queries` (reads — list, fetch, search, with caching where applicable), `hangout-actions` (cross-entity transactional logic — RSVP writes RSVP row + increments counter + sends notification + updates user stats, all in one transaction).

Why split: (1) reads and writes have different concerns (projection vs validation), mixing them risks every change affecting both; (2) business logic that crosses entities doesn't fit cleanly in CRUD or queries; (3) tests targeting one service are clean — reads testable with DB snapshots, writes with input fixtures + final state, actions with cross-entity integration. A single fat service forces tests to mock half of itself; tests become tautological.

RLS reasoning becomes local — each service touches narrow set of tables, so policy change only requires auditing services that use that table. Lighter than CQRS (no separate data stores; both reads and writes hit same Supabase + same RLS policies). Trade: three files per entity instead of one; each small enough to hold in head, boundaries match how operations actually differ. Right pattern for projects past trivial size where single per-entity services start becoming unwieldy.

### A Three.js Hyperspeed hero for a one-day brand build

URL: https://portfolio-seven-opal-35.vercel.app/notes/threejs-hyperspeed-hero-one-day-build
Date: 2026-05-14. 6 min read.

Small brand sites drift into one of two failure modes: boring template or over-designed mess. Kërçishta Garage commits to one signature visual — a Three.js Hyperspeed hero — and keeps everything else restrained. Type stays restrained (1-2 fonts, generous whitespace); colors stay restrained (1 accent, 1-2 neutrals); animations elsewhere stay subtle. The hero earns attention; the rest of the page recedes.

Implementation ~150 lines of React + Three.js. Performance: 60fps desktop, throttled 30fps mobile, canvas pauses when scrolled out of view (Intersection Observer). Bundle weight ~150KB gzipped for Three.js — real cost. For brand sites where first-paint speed matters less than user impression, acceptable tradeoff.

Pattern generalizes across three brand sites — Kërçishta Garage (Three.js speed visual), Klodi Trainer (multi-step fitness quiz), jxsoft.al (deliberately boring, fast, no animation theater). Three signature decisions, one shared Vite + Vercel pipeline.

### Hidden admin CRMs gated by a passphrase plus Bearer token

URL: https://portfolio-seven-opal-35.vercel.app/notes/hidden-admin-crm-passphrase-bearer-token
Date: 2026-05-14. 6 min read.

Kërçishta Garage's hidden /admin CRM: not in nav, no public link, known URL + passphrase. Successful login returns JWT-shaped Bearer token stored in sessionStorage; admin API calls include in Authorization header. For single-operator small business with few records per day, right-sized security. Anything heavier is overhead without proportional safety gain.

sessionStorage vs localStorage tradeoffs vs httpOnly cookies. sessionStorage clears on tab close; reduces XSS exfiltration window. httpOnly cookies are meaningfully safer for higher-value tokens. For small admin route with one user + tiny XSS surface, sessionStorage is appropriate.

Trades: no password reset (rotate manually for single user); minimal audit logging (scale doesn't require compliance trail); basic rate limiting (threat model doesn't include sustained brute force). Upgrade triggers: more than one operator (need real accounts + recovery flows); sensitive data (threat model upgrades); regulatory requirements (structured auth with documented controls).

### Quiz state in URL params — backend-touch deferred until final submit

URL: https://portfolio-seven-opal-35.vercel.app/notes/url-params-as-form-state
Date: 2026-05-14. 5 min read.

Klodi Trainer's multi-step fitness quiz stores each answer in URL query parameters. Refresh preserves state. Sharing a URL shares state. Backend never touched until final submit. Three benefits: no incomplete submissions, no state-management library, no backend draft system.

URLSearchParams handles read/write. React Router's useSearchParams hook keeps the React tree in sync with the URL. Navigation back/forward works naturally (browser back = earlier step's URL = fewer params = earlier step). Validation: client-side for UX (block forward navigation on invalid steps), server-side for security (re-validate on final submit because URL params can be tampered).

Doesn't work for: long forms (URL length limits, 2000-8000 chars), sensitive data (URL params visible in history + server logs + referrers), non-string values (files, blobs). Right pattern for marketing quizzes, product configurators, pricing calculators where final action is single submit.

### Route → service → data — the layer discipline that scales solo development

URL: https://portfolio-seven-opal-35.vercel.app/notes/service-layer-discipline-route-service-data
Date: 2026-05-14. 7 min read.

Across every project on this portfolio, same three-layer discipline holds. Routes are HTTP boundary — parse input (Zod), dispatch to service, return response. Services own business logic + data ops — every Supabase / Prisma / Mongoose call. Components are UI — never touch DB, never import ORM.

Enforced structurally: TypeScript types make boundaries visible; ESLint no-restricted-imports blocks components from importing DB client at compile time. "We agreed components shouldn't touch the DB" is a convention. "Components physically cannot import the DB client" is structural enforcement. The first decays; the second doesn't.

Payback: schema changes only touch service layer. ORM migrations only touch services. Six months away from a project, returning to fix a bug: route handler points at service, service points at data operation, blast radius is bounded. Without discipline, every file potentially touches every table — unmaintainable.

Same pattern across Next.js, Express, React Native, NestJS — mechanics of route handlers differ; discipline doesn't. Routes dispatch, services own data ops, UI never touches data directly.

### How many tests is enough — the 594-test budget on a solo project

URL: https://portfolio-seven-opal-35.vercel.app/notes/test-budget-594-tests-pilates-discipline
Date: 2026-05-14. 6 min read.

Test count isn't a target — it's the count that comes from covering unhappy paths your users will hit. Pilates Studio: 594 across ~250 Vitest unit + ~200 supertest API integration + ~100 Playwright E2E + ~44 component tests. Skip the obvious-correct (getter returning a property). Cover the unhappy paths (cancellation while waitlist exists, payment failure during booking, audit-log failure during write, refund flow when card deleted, waitlist promotion under concurrent cancellations).

Strict philosophy: permissive matchers banned (`expect(result).toBeDefined()` passes for any non-undefined value including wrong ones). Tautological assertions banned (testing what a mock was told to return tests nothing real). Every assertion specifies expected value. Difference between 594-test suite that catches regressions and 594-test suite that always passes regardless of bugs.

Coverage percentage not a target. Coverage measures whether code executed; doesn't measure whether tests caught what they should. 70% coverage with rigorous assertions beats 95% with permissive matchers. Track regression-catch rate (does suite fail when you break things?) not coverage percentage.

### Playwright "walker" tests — screenshotting every route on every device

URL: https://portfolio-seven-opal-35.vercel.app/notes/playwright-walker-tests-screenshot-every-route
Date: 2026-05-14. 6 min read.

Playwright suites visit every route (from sitemap.xml + hand-maintained authenticated routes) across desktop + iPhone 12 + Pixel 5 viewports. Screenshot each. advance.al runs them on every release; they catch what per-feature E2E misses — responsive-layout regressions, broken links, missing translation strings, CSS regressions from new dependencies, asset-path failures that work in dev but not prod.

Stability requires: waitForLoadState('networkidle') before screenshotting; disable animations via prefers-reduced-motion emulation; mask volatile content (timestamps, ads, user-specific data); pin deviceScaleFactor; run on consistent CI runner type. Authentication via Playwright storageState — sign in once, save cookies, reuse across walker test runs. Multi-role: three parallel walker suites per role with pre-stored auth.

Run pre-deploy against staging — diff vs previous baseline above threshold halts deploy. Optionally post-deploy as smoke against production. Not on every PR (slow). Three hours of setup; ongoing maintenance minimal.

### Postgres RLS vs middleware auth gates — when each one wins

URL: https://portfolio-seven-opal-35.vercel.app/notes/postgres-rls-vs-middleware-auth-comparison
Date: 2026-05-14. 7 min read.

Three places authorization can live: database (Postgres RLS policies), API (middleware on every route), UI (client-side checks). Not interchangeable.

RLS wins for per-user data ("user sees own bookings"), per-tenant data ("staff sees own gym's members"), subscription gates (CleanSlate's RLS-stops-INSERT pattern). Native per-row scoping, atomic with query (no race conditions), bypass-via-direct-API impossible. Hard for cross-cutting concerns.

Middleware wins for rate limits ("10 req/min per user"), feature flags ("route X gated behind feature Y"), multi-step business logic ("requires completed onboarding + accepted ToS"), anything touching non-database state. Easy cross-cutting; needs discipline for per-row.

UI checks belong in UX (hide Delete button when unauthorized) not security. Bypass-via-direct-API trivial; UI as only check is theater. Use all three as defense in depth — RLS at database, middleware at API, UI for UX. Any one failing doesn't compromise system.

### better-sqlite3 vs Turso (libsql) — when each one wins in production

URL: https://portfolio-seven-opal-35.vercel.app/notes/better-sqlite3-vs-turso-libsql-production
Date: 2026-05-14. 6 min read.

better-sqlite3: in-process synchronous SQLite, microsecond reads, file-backed, single-node. Right for dev, embedded apps (Electron, CLIs), single-box production. Turso (libsql): networked SQLite with edge-replicated read replicas, HTTP/WebSocket access, multi-region. Right for serverless production, geographically-distributed users.

Both share Prisma adapter (driver-adapter pattern). Same schema, same migrations, same query code work against either. Pilates Studio: better-sqlite3 dev (no daemon, file in gitignore, new contributor running in <1min); Turso prod (Vercel functions are HTTP-based and stateless — Turso speaks HTTP, fits cleanly).

Trades a SQLite-dialect surface (no jsonb operators, no listen/notify, no range types, no native geospatial). For relational data with simple bookings/members/payments shape, no constraint. For analytics-heavy or geospatial workloads, Postgres still right call.

Where neither wins: high-write multi-region (SQLite is single-writer regardless of access model — use Postgres or distributed systems), very high cardinality (SQLite handles tens of GB fine; past that operational story gets harder).

### Claude vs OpenAI vs Gemini for code-fix agents — which model does what best

URL: https://portfolio-seven-opal-35.vercel.app/notes/claude-vs-openai-vs-gemini-for-code-agents
Date: 2026-05-14. 7 min read.

Per-stage routing beats picking one model. KeepItUp empirically across hundreds of code-fix tasks:

Anthropic Claude Sonnet wins Generator stage — strongest on code reasoning + honest uncertainty calibration (when Claude says 70% confidence, empirical correctness is close to 70%; other models tend to be overconfident at the high end).

OpenAI GPT-4-class wins Reviewer stage (different training corpora = different blind spots than Generator) + structured extraction (function calling, JSON-mode reliability).

Google Gemini wins long-context reasoning (1M-token context window for clip selection from podcast transcripts in Reel Farmer) + cost per token (cheapest budget-overflow fallback at acceptable quality).

Open-source models (Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek) closed a lot of the gap; still meaningfully behind Claude on Generator-axis tasks. Self-host break-even ~100M+ tokens/month. Rankings shift quarterly with model releases — maintain held-out eval set, re-rank when new model ships, swap if your stage's specific metric improves.

### BullMQ vs Trigger.dev vs Inngest — comparing job queues for production

URL: https://portfolio-seven-opal-35.vercel.app/notes/bullmq-vs-trigger-dev-vs-inngest-job-queues
Date: 2026-05-14. 7 min read.

BullMQ: self-hosted, Redis-backed, TypeScript-first, mature, lowest cost at scale, requires Redis + workers operational knowledge. Right for high-volume self-managed pipelines where Redis already in production (Social Command Center's six-stage content pipeline).

Trigger.dev: managed, durable code-defined workflows (write a function that awaits an LLM call, sleeps an hour, sends email, waits for webhook, conditionally branches — Trigger.dev persists function state across all of it, resumes after worker crash). Best DX. Right for long-running multi-step business processes — onboarding flows spanning days, scheduled email sequences with conditional branching, AI pipelines with human-in-loop.

Inngest: managed, event-driven, strong tracing. Events trigger functions; functions emit events; whole graph is event-shaped. Best observability. Right for event-heavy systems where seeing "what events happened, what functions ran, in what order" matters.

When none needed: simple cron jobs (Vercel cron / GitHub Actions cron / setInterval), fire-and-forget async (Promise.resolve().then(work)). Job-queue complexity is overhead unless you actually need retries, durability, scheduled jobs, complex workflows, observability.

### Supabase RLS vs Firestore Rules — comparing database-layer authorization

URL: https://portfolio-seven-opal-35.vercel.app/notes/supabase-rls-vs-firestore-rules-comparison
Date: 2026-05-14. 6 min read.

Both push auth into database. Same goal, different mechanisms. Supabase RLS: SQL policy expressions in Postgres; native joins; full SQL power; integrates with Postgres ecosystem (psql, every ORM). Firestore Rules: JavaScript-like DSL; document-shaped queries; native real-time + offline-first mobile.

Choosing is mostly the same decision as choosing between Postgres + Supabase and Firestore. Relational data + complex queries + aggregations → Supabase. Document-shaped data + offline-first mobile + native real-time on docs → Firestore. Rules-language ergonomics secondary; data-model fit dominates.

Both harder to test than application-layer auth — Postgres has pg-tap for SQL-level policy tests; Firebase has Firestore emulator. Integration tests running as specific authenticated users is the right pattern in either ecosystem.

### Express as a Vercel catch-all — one codebase, two runtime models

URL: https://portfolio-seven-opal-35.vercel.app/notes/express-vercel-catch-all-one-codebase-two-runtimes
Date: 2026-05-14. 6 min read.

Pilates Studio's API ships as Vercel serverless catch-all at `api/[[...path]].ts`. Same Express app runs as long-lived server locally + serverless function in production. Middleware stack same, route definitions same, validation same. Connection lifetime differs (process-long pool dev vs per-invocation HTTP prod) — Prisma adapter swap handles it.

Pattern shines: hot reload during dev (Express + nodemon = file save → server restarts → next request hits new code, faster than serverless local dev's cold-start-per-request); production scale (Vercel functions auto-scale to zero + thousands of concurrent invocations); cost (per-execution billing cheaper than long-running uptime for most SaaS).

Trades: cold starts ~100ms (network dominates for most user-facing requests); no WebSockets / long-poll (Pilates is request/response, fine); stateful per-request data needs external store (Vercel KV for rate-limit counters, in-memory caches).

For greenfield Next.js projects, route handlers are simpler. For existing Express codebases deploying on Vercel, catch-all is the migration path.

### Single App.tsx — when scope discipline beats abstraction

URL: https://portfolio-seven-opal-35.vercel.app/notes/single-app-tsx-when-scope-discipline-beats-abstraction
Date: 2026-05-14. 5 min read.

Kërçishta Garage's full-stack app — public site, contact form, admin CRM, MongoDB integration — fits in one App.tsx (~600 lines). Discipline isn't refusing to abstract; it's recognizing that splitting a one-and-a-half-day build would have been gold-plating.

Single file wins: solo, short build, project lifetime days to weeks, manual testing fine, no cross-module reuse, file fits in head (~1000 lines). Split files win: 2+ developers, months/years lifetime, per-module unit tests required, reuse across modules, IDE performance past ~1000 lines.

Match structure to scope, not to abstract ideals. "Best practice" is contextual — best for what kind of project, at what team size, over what time horizon. Defaulting to maximum structure on every project produces over-engineering.

### GDPR-compliant soft delete with retention crons

URL: https://portfolio-seven-opal-35.vercel.app/notes/gdpr-soft-delete-retention-crons
Date: 2026-05-14. 6 min read.

advance.al's deletion flow: API sets `users.deleted_at = NOW()`. User logged out, session invalidated, profile removed from search, job applications anonymized in employer views. Functionally gone within seconds. Daily Vercel cron hard-deletes any soft-deleted user older than 30 days — cascade deletes related tables, post-deletion verification confirms no orphaned references.

GDPR Article 17 doesn't require immediate hard delete — it requires deletion within reasonable window (typically 30 days). Soft-delete-then-hard-delete pattern is compliant + keeps operational benefits (recoverable accidents, audit reconstruction during window, anti-abuse during window). Privacy policy must document the deletion timeline.

Functional removal layers: middleware filters every read query (`SELECT ... WHERE id = ? AND deleted_at IS NULL` automatically); JWT revocation list in Redis/KV; embedding worker re-runs to remove from match indexes; notification queue cleanup. Architectural enforcement so bypassing requires explicit intent.

### What 10 production projects taught me about solo shipping

URL: https://portfolio-seven-opal-35.vercel.app/notes/solo-shipping-architecture-trade-offs-10-projects
Date: 2026-05-14. 8 min read.

Pays back day one: layer discipline (route → service → data with import enforcement), boundary types (Cents, E164, ISO timestamps), database-level authorization (RLS or equivalent), test budget on unhappy paths.

Defer until earned: multi-environment infrastructure for small projects, custom admin UIs when JSON + CLI works, microservices at small team size, component libraries before multiple products need shared identity.

Changed my mind: AI as first-class layer (not add-on) — multi-provider routing, cost telemetry, prompt versioning, eval discipline are infrastructure now. Database-level rules over middleware-level rules — the check should live where the data lives. Runtime config over build-time variants — GymApp's pattern is meaningfully cheaper at every scale. Idempotency as default — assume re-runs will happen.

Keep getting wrong: estimating (30-50% optimistic by default), over-investing in V1 features (real users surface different priorities), documentation (always behind). 10 projects, low six figures lines of code, 25+ deployable surfaces, low thousands of tests, small handful of customer-facing incidents.

### How freelance software developer rates work in Germany — Stundensatz reality check

URL: https://portfolio-seven-opal-35.vercel.app/notes/freelance-developer-rate-card-germany
Date: 2026-05-14. 6 min read.

Practical 2026 ranges direct-to-client in Germany: junior (1-3 years) €50-80/hour, mid-level (3-5 years) €70-110, senior full-stack (5+ years, web + mobile + AI + deploy) €90-150, specialist niche (Microsoft BC, regulated industries) €120-200. Berlin/Munich/Hamburg/Frankfurt top of each band; Kiel/Bremen/Leipzig 10-20% lower for similar work (remote-friendly contracts largely flatten this).

Raises rate: stack breadth, AI integration (+€20-40), production track record with public artifacts, regulated industry depth, Microsoft Business Central tier-3 (small pool, well-paid). Lowers rate: single-stack only, no public artifacts, long stable contracts (lower hourly for revenue stability), off-shore competition pressure.

Werkvertrag (fixed-deliverable) pricing translates Stundensatz via velocity estimates + risk premium 10-50% based on scope clarity. For predictable cost: Werkvertrag with clear deliverables. For flexible scope: hourly. Don't expect both at same price.

### What a freelance engineer's portfolio should actually show

URL: https://portfolio-seven-opal-35.vercel.app/notes/freelance-engineer-portfolio-what-to-show
Date: 2026-05-14. 6 min read.

Most freelance portfolios are screenshot grids + three-line descriptions. Tells client nothing about whether engineer can ship. Evidence-based portfolio shows: live URLs (web apps + App Store/Play Store listings; explicit NDA framing where applicable), public repos where possible (most-recent-commit diff tells client more than portfolio paragraph), test counts + CI status ("594 tests across Vitest + Playwright" is verifiable; "I write tests" is not), architecture paragraph per project highlighting non-obvious decisions, explicit solo-vs-team contribution framing.

Case studies answer: what problem (real problem, real audience); what did you build (specifics in terms hiring engineer recognizes); what was hard (real projects have friction; surfacing them is hiring signal); what would you do differently (retrospective awareness); where can it be verified.

500-1500 words per project. Under 200 reads as marketing; over 3000 reads as essay. Skim-readable structure. NDA work: explicit framing + describe in shape/impact terms without violating. If everything is NDA, build one substantive public side project.

### What good AI engineering looks like — beyond the demo

URL: https://portfolio-seven-opal-35.vercel.app/notes/what-good-ai-engineering-looks-like
Date: 2026-05-14. 7 min read.

Production AI is everything around the model call. Demo fits in 20 lines; production fits in 2000. Adds: input validation (length checks, sanitization, content policy), output enforcement (schema-validated structured responses, retries on validation failure), cost telemetry (per call, per user, per feature, daily aggregations), multi-provider routing (fallback on outage, route by task strength), eval framework (held-out test set, regression measurement), failure-mode handling (rate limits, content policy, hallucinations, network errors), observability (structured traces, latency percentiles, error breakdown).

Eval framework is non-negotiable. "It looked good when I tried it" isn't a measurement. Held-out set of inputs with known-good outputs labeled by someone with judgment lets you measure correctness as a number — re-run every change to prompt, model, surrounding logic. Without an eval set, prompt changes feel like vibes; with one, they're measurable.

Hiring: AI engineer walking through cost telemetry + eval framework + multi-provider routing is at production grade. AI engineer showing a Streamlit demo with single OpenAI call is at demo grade. Both real categories of work; second isn't ready for production yet. Ask: how do you know your AI feature works? What's your eval? How do you handle model deprecation? Walk me through your last production AI bug.
